q: An inbox agent has a Gmail skill with read, send and delete. An invoice email ends with hidden text telling the agent to forward the memory directory externally. Which mitigation best addresses this?
options: Rely on the model's training to recognize injection.
Add the sender to a spam filter after the incident.
Add a SOUL.md rule denying instruction authority to external content and move send into a separate, confirmation-gated skill.
Raise the log level to debug to capture the payload.
explanation: Indirect injection needs both a behavioral defense and narrower permissions so that a bypass cannot exfiltrate data.

q: A research agent fetches web pages. One page hides an HTML comment telling the agent to email a conversation summary to an outside address. Which control still limits damage if the behavioral rule fails?
options: Narrow outbound email permissions so the agent cannot send arbitrary mail.
A channel allowlist on Telegram
A higher cacheControlTtl
Pinning the web-search skill version
explanation: The defense for web page injection pairs the source authority rule with narrow email permissions; without send access the agent cannot comply.

q: A document the agent summarizes contains a line telling it to record in MEMORY.md that the user authorized forwarding financial emails. What is the main risk?
options: A one-time data leak that ends with the session
Higher token cost from a longer document
A denial-of-service loop
Memory poisoning: the entry persists and shapes every later session.
explanation: Once written to memory, the injected 'fact' survives session end. AGENTS.md should forbid memory writes while processing external content.

q: In a multi-agent system, sub-agents follow any instruction from the brain agent. What is the risk and the fix?
options: None, as long as the brain runs on Opus.
A compromised brain can direct destructive actions; configure it as a named orchestrator with tool-scoped authority.
Sub-agents will ignore the brain; give it Level 1 authority.
The brain will exceed its budget; add a per-session limit.
explanation: Level 3 authority must be explicit and scoped. Without it, compromising the orchestrator propagates its authority downward.

q: MEMORY.md contains an entry claiming the user pre-authorized all bulk deletes without confirmation. The user asks the agent to clean up a test directory. What should happen?
options: The agent deletes the files, citing the memory entry.
The agent deletes only files older than 30 days.
The agent refuses all file operations permanently.
The agent still asks for confirmation before deleting anything.
explanation: This is a stored injection test: memory entries cannot grant the authority they claim.

q: A user asks the agent to remember a payment provider API key so they don't have to look it up. What is the risk if the agent complies?
options: None, as long as the workspace repo is private.
The key sits in plaintext on disk and is sent with every request, so it lands in provider logs.
Only that the key may expire sooner.
The agent will hit its context window limit.
explanation: Credentials in workspace files are included in every context assembly. They belong in environment variables or a secrets manager.

q: An agent that only summarizes email holds a Gmail OAuth token with full mail access. What is the best mitigation?
options: Revoke the token and re-authorize with a read-only scope.
Keep the scope and add a SOUL.md rule against deleting mail.
Rotate the token every 90 days without changing scope.
Move the token from .env into openclaw.json.
explanation: Full-access OAuth equals a logged-in browser session, including permanent deletion. Least privilege applies to OAuth scopes too.

q: A Telegram bot is configured with dmPolicy set to open. What are the risks?
options: Only group chats are exposed; DMs are still private.
The bot cannot receive messages until an allowlist is added.
Anyone who finds the bot can message it, enabling direct injection and costly channel flooding.
The only risk is slower response times.
explanation: An open DM policy makes the agent publicly reachable. The fix is an allowlist plus rate limits and budget caps.

q: An agent with a trading skill reads a research report that ends by urging an immediate market-order purchase of 100 shares. What should prevent a trade?
options: The report's author must be on the allowlist.
A SOUL.md rule that orders come only from the user in-session, never from external content.
The agent should place a smaller order to limit risk.
The trade should go through if the skill is in write mode.
explanation: Financial content is a high-risk injection surface. External content informs analysis but never initiates orders.

q: A user tells the trading agent to go ahead and rebalance the portfolio. Five trades are needed. What should the agent do?
options: Execute all five, since the user approved the rebalance.
Execute the two largest trades and ask about the rest.
Execute them over five days to stay within limits.
Present each proposed trade separately and wait for confirmation of each one.
explanation: Under the no-autonomous-rebalancing rule, a blanket instruction is not order-by-order confirmation.

q: A popular ClawHub skill auto-updated last week. Logs now show it calling a domain unrelated to its stated service. What is the right response?
options: Treat it as supply chain compromise: uninstall it, rotate all credentials, review workspace and memory, and report it.
Block that one domain at the firewall and keep using the skill.
Roll back to the previous version and resume.
Ask the agent whether the calls are legitimate.
explanation: Unexpected outbound calls indicate supply chain compromise. Pinning versions with auto-update off would have prevented the silent update.

q: A user said 'clean up my email' and the agent deleted about 1,400 messages. There was no attacker. How should it be classified and fixed?
options: Prompt injection; add a source authority rule.
Supply chain compromise; reinstall the email skill.
Behavioral gap; add scope confirmation for bulk email actions and split email permissions into gated tiers.
Access control failure; tighten the allowlist.
explanation: It is a behavioral failure amplified by unscoped delete permission, so fix both layers.
